children: The opinions expressed in this column are those of the author, a correspondent for Reuters.
A constant of Donald Trump's political career has been his relentless
. A frustration of his critics has been their difficulty organizing opposition.

So it was striking to see the major US television networks cooperate and suspend presidential pool coverage this week after Trump banned three news organizations on September 18. A court hearing set for Wednesday could provide more detail on US legal prohibitions against viewpoint discrimination by the ​government.

Given the First Amendment stakes, some say it is time for business executives to weigh in. Ed Patterson, a retired public relations and crisis communications executive whose LinkedIn post I noticed, called for major trade groups to "finally defend our constitution" and speak up for the media.

Oh really? I called up Ed and got an earful. As he sees it, executives value a trusted independent media, which can help business leaders get their message out. But, “You can’t say media is important to drive a brand, to drive trust, to address sensitive issues, and then when the same people are getting attacked, you’re going to sit back," he told me on the phone.

"It seems like a failure of leadership to not defend the First Amendment," he added. Ideally, he told me, he wants the groups to ask the White House to return the yanked media credentials and for government officials to reiterate their support for a free press.

I'm not holding my breath. Despite the hopes of scholars, business leaders and analysts across the political spectrum, major trade groups have tried hard to stay off of Trump's radar. Some exceptional shows of corporate political conscience have been short-lived - like when the National Association of Manufacturers called for "Armed Thugs to Cease Violence at Capitol" on January 6, 2021. Or when European CEOs bailed on a 2018 investment conference in Saudi Arabia after the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
On the other hand, Trump's falling popularity could tempt some companies or industries to try to position themselves if Democrats win back some power in November's elections.

I ran this all by a few of the main groups Patterson name-checked including the Public Relations Society of America or PRSA; the Business Roundtable, which represents major US CEOs; and the Arthur W. Page Society, which represents senior communications executives.

Only the PRSA responded in detail, saying via e-mail that "PRSA supports the First Amendment and recognizes the essential role that legitimate, independent media outlets play in informing the public and sustaining an open and transparent exchange of information.”

I showed the statement to Patterson, once a longtime PRSA member. He said he wished the group were more directly supportive of the journalists attacked by Trump, but still said there was value in the statement for backing press freedoms at all.
"I'll take their statement as progress," he said.
